findings.printedLatin: Cum vero delectatio carnis per consensum usque ad interiora animae penetrat, tunc nimirum cor hostium ad Deum intrinsecus praesidentem clausit, ut jam ipse importuno strepitu commotus de illa sua quiete exsurgens dicat.
findings.englishAsRendered: But when the delight of the flesh penetrates through consent even to the inner parts of the soul, then assuredly the heart of the foes closed toward God presiding within, so that now he himself, stirred by the importunate din, rising up out of that quiet of his, may say.
findings.conjecture: clamavit for clausit — the lemma verb: 'cor hostium ad Deum intrinsecus praesidentem CLAMAVIT'
findings.whyContradiction: The lemma being expounded is 'CLAMAVIT cor eorum ad Dominum,' and the same clause's own purpose-clause requires a cry, not a closing: 'ut jam ipse importuno STREPITU commotus de illa sua quiete exsurgens dicat: Clamor Sodomorum... multiplicatus est.' Two lines earlier the contrast is set in the same terms — 'si tamen non admittuntur, in consensum intro, AD AURES USQUE DEI NON PERTINGUNT' — so when consent IS given the noise does reach God's ears. 'clausit' also has no object and cannot govern 'ad Deum'; 'clamavit ad Deum' is the printed idiom of the lemma. Our English carried the defect literally ('closed toward God'), which is correct practice, but the crux is unlogged and the paragraph now denies the very cry it is glossing.

findings.printedLatin: quia, dum populo Dei propter peccata ejus dominari permittuntur, divinae potentiae derogant: et hoc eum prohiberi non posse existimant, quod ipso permittente, et disponente fieri ignorant.
findings.englishAsRendered: because, while they are permitted to hold dominion over the people of God on account of its sins, they detract from the divine power: and they judge that this cannot be hindered which they know not comes to pass by his own permitting and disposing.
findings.conjecture: prohibere for prohiberi — 'hoc eum prohibere non posse existimant', i.e. they think that HE (God) is unable to prevent this
findings.whyContradiction: The immediately preceding clause states the charge: 'divinae potentiae DEROGANT' — they detract from the divine POWER. Detraction from God's power is the claim that God CANNOT STOP them (active); the printed passive 'eum prohiberi non posse' says instead that HE cannot be hindered, which is an affirmation of divine power and the opposite of the charge just laid. The closing relative confirms the intended sense — what they are ignorant of is that it happens 'ipso permittente et disponente', i.e. that God is in control after all. Secondary, on OUR side: the English silently drops the accusative 'eum' and makes 'hoc' the subject ('this cannot be hindered'), which is neither the printed reading nor the required one and smooths away the agency question entirely.

findings.printedLatin: Aperuerunt, inquit, super te os suum omnes inimici tui. Apertio oris tui crudelitatem et subsannationem designat. Aperuerunt os avidi ad devorandum. Aperuerunt os superbi ad subsannandum.
findings.englishAsRendered: They have opened, he says, their mouth over thee, all thy enemies. The opening of thy mouth designates cruelty and derision. The greedy have opened the mouth to devour. The proud have opened the mouth to deride.
findings.conjecture: oris eorum (or bare 'oris') for oris tui — eye-skip from the 'inimici TUI' of the lemma immediately above
findings.whyContradiction: The lemma the gloss expounds makes the mouth the enemies': 'Aperuerunt super te OS SUUM omnes inimici tui,' and the two sentences that follow assign the opening to them and to nobody else — 'Aperuerunt os AVIDI ad devorandum. Aperuerunt os SUPERBI ad subsannandum.' The addressee (the daughter of Sion) is throughout this paragraph the one derided and devoured, never the derider, so an 'apertio oris TUI' that 'designates cruelty and derision' assigns the cruelty to the victim. Our English carries the printed pronoun literally, so the defect is the plate's; it is simply unlogged.

findings.printedLatin: quando ratione faciendi malum tibi persuadebant, falsa viderunt; quando vero etiam ad irrationabiles actus cupiditate victam impellebant, non solum falsa et stulta viderunt.
findings.englishAsRendered: when by a reason for acting they persuaded thee to evil, they saw false things; but when they drove thee, conquered by cupidity, even to irrational acts, they saw not only false but also foolish things.
findings.conjecture: non solum falsa, SED ETIAM stulta viderunt — the correlative's second limb is missing, 'et' standing where 'sed etiam' belongs
findings.whyContradiction: The two-limb structure is explicit: the first limb has 'falsa viderunt' (false only), so the second limb exists precisely to ADD 'stulta'. As printed, 'non solum falsa et stulta viderunt' negates the pair the sentence is built to affirm — it denies that they saw false-and-foolish things, in a clause introduced to say they saw the worse of the two. Hugh's own formula for the same distinction stands a column earlier at 0294A: 'promissiones autem NON SOLUM falsas, SED ET stultas nominat.' Our English carries the printed words but silently repairs the correlative to 'not only false but also foolish', supplying 'sed etiam' the plate does not print — so this defect is concealed rather than reproduced.

findings.printedLatin: non solum falsa et stulta viderunt.
findings.englishAsRendered: they saw not only false but also foolish things.
findings.conjecture: Render the printed connective: 'they saw not only false and foolish things.' The plate prints 'et'; 'sed etiam' is supplied by us.
findings.whyContradiction: This is a silent repair of the plate defect logged directly above, and the crux entry for this very site asserts the opposite about our text: cruces-0010.md at 0296C states 'Rendered exactly as printed, non carried, NOTHING SUPPLIED (Pattern 7a).' The English in src/english/11058/0011.md in fact supplies the missing correlative — 'not only false BUT ALSO foolish' — restoring the climax the plate lost and leaving no lexical trace that the correlative was broken. Per translation-style.md 7a a crux that records a defect does not license under-rendering it: 'The crux records; the text reproduces. Both, or the entry is incomplete.' Fix is one word: 'and' for 'but also'.

findings.printedLatin: Murus filiae Sion unumquemque veritatis defensorem significare potest, si per quem cor inimicorum clamat ad Dominum;
findings.englishAsRendered: The wall of the daughter of Sion can signify each several defender of the truth, if through whom the heart of the enemies cries to the Lord;
findings.conjecture: super quem for si per quem — 'unumquemque veritatis defensorem ... SUPER QUEM cor inimicorum clamat ad Dominum'
findings.whyContradiction: The lemma is 'Clamavit cor eorum ad Dominum SUPER MURUM filiae Sion,' and the gloss identifies the wall with the defender; the relative must therefore reproduce 'super murum' as 'super quem' — the defender is what they cry OVER, in triumph, which is exactly what the following clause describes ('cum non solum simplices quosque in Ecclesia, sed ipsos etiam defensores veritatis ad suos errores convertunt'). The printed 'per quem' makes the defender the instrument THROUGH WHICH the enemies cry, binding the agency to the wrong party. Logged low because the printed 'si per quem' is broken rather than merely inverted; note also that our English renders it as untagged nonsense ('if through whom') with no [sic:] marker.
